anchorLine: ἀνθρωπεία ἐν αὐτῷ οὐχ ἤνωτο (p), λέγεται ἀγνοεῖν.
text: (p) Ἐν αὐτῷ οὐχ ἤνωτο. Necessario addidi negat, ut oppositio constaret ἡνώθη καὶ οὐχ ἤνωτο, et quod una hæc solutionum sit difficillimi ejus loci Mar. xiii. Sic Greg. Theol., iii, De theol.: Γινώσκει μὲν ὡς Θεός· ἀγνοεῖν δέ φησιν ὡς ἄνθρωπος, ἄν τις τὸ φαινόμενον χωρίσῃ τοῦ νοουμένου· Cognoscit ut Deus. Ait vero ignorare ut homo est, si quis quod oculis conspicuum est separaverit, ab eo quod mente intelligitur. Mente scilicet ac subtili cogitatu, intelligendo quod vi sua habet homo, et quod ex unione cum Verbo. Et, ut Basil. loquitur: Ἐὰν μέντοι ἰσχναῖς ἐπινοίαις, ἦτον νοῦ λεπταῖς φαντασίαις, διέλῃς τὸ κτιστὸν ἐκ τοῦ ἀκτίστου, δούλη καὶ ἀγνοοῦσά ἐστιν ἡ σὰρξ καὶ ψυχὴ τοῦ Κυρίου, εἰ μὴ ἤνωτο τῷ Θεοῦ Λόγῳ· Si tamen subtilibus cogitationibus mentisque acutis rationibus creatum ab increato diviseris, serva est ac ignorans Domini caro et anima, si non esset unita Dei Verbo. Ubi lepide Cord. intellectualibus vestigiis, quod male ἰσχναῖς legerit ac repræsentet. Alia, eaque pervulgata solutio est, ut ad Patrem tanquam auctorem, id quod scit, Christus referat; dicaturque solus Pater scire, quod Filius non nisi cum Patre, et ut Pater, atque ab illo sciat. Sic Theol. glossat, Οὐδὲ ὁ Υἱὸς ἄλλως οἶδε τὴν ἡμέραν ἢ τὴν ὥραν, ἢ ὡς ὁ Πατήρ· Neque Filius, aliter scilicet novit diem aut horam, quam sicut Pater. Basil. Ἀλλ' οὐδ' ὁ Υἱὸς ἔγνω, εἰ μὴ ὁ Πατήρ· ἐκ γὰρ τοῦ Πατρὸς αὐτῷ ὑπῆρχε δεδομένη ἡ γνῶσις· At neque Filius (subaudi nosset) nisi Pater. A Patre enim illi data cognitio erat. Nec apte satis Cord. At neque Filius novit nisi Pater, quo nihil lucis Marci textui accedit. At neque in eo saniór Corderii versio, quod urget Basilius, datamque solutionem non videri violentam ostendit, ἐπειδὴ οὐ πρόσκειται, τὸ, μόνος, ὡς καὶ παρὰ τῷ Ματθαίῳ. Cord. Cum addatur adjunctum solus, quod apud Matthæum jacet. Nempe jacet (elegans scilicet) voluit pro, positum est; exciditque negatio, uti solet, vel festinanti calamo, vel prelo. Tertia denique, quod hæc, κατ' οἰκονομίαν certaque dispensatione dicta sint, qua Dominus discipulos avocabat a quæstionibus in quibus plus esset curiositatis, quam necessariæ utilitatis; cum alioqui diligenter edissereret, si quid percontarentur, τῶν ὅσα ἦν φιλομαθείας ἔχοντα δόξαν, inquit Cyril. eorum quæ honestæ cupiditatis sciendi speciem haberent, nec tamen altiori scrutatione egerent. Συντέλειαν itaque commodum præterit, se nescire, καθὸ ἄνθρωπος: qua homo; at neque sanctos angelos in cælo, inquit, ἵνα μὴ λυπῶνται, ὡς μὴ θαρρηθέντες τὸ μέτριον. Ne inde dolerent, quod quæ modum non excederent illis credita non essent. Id enim θαρρεῖν τὸ ἄῤῥητον, arcanum credere seu committere, apud Chrys. I Cor. aliosque. Scrupulosiorque Henr. Steph. qui malit: Audeo committere. Per quam inscite Cord.: Ne contristentur, tanquam supra modum dissidentes; pigebitque cum Latinis istiusmodi interpretum etiam Græca recensere, eaque ad manum habere? Isid. l. 1, epist. 127. Nullam utilitatem ostendit, quod quis eum diem aut horam sciat; maximam vero, quod nesciat, Ἵνα πᾶσαν ἡμέραν ἐκείνην εἶναι νομίζοντες, ἕτοιμοι πρὸς ταύτην τυγχάνωμεν· Ut omnem diem, illum esse existimantes, parati ad eum simus.
en: I added "he denies" of necessity, so that the contrast "was united" and "was not united" would stand, and because this is one of the solutions to that very difficult passage, Mark 13. So Gregory the Theologian says: he knows as God, but says he is ignorant as man, if one separates what appears from what is understood. That is, by mind and subtle thought one grasps what the man has by his own power and what he has by union with the Word. And as Basil puts it: if you divide the created from the uncreated by fine conceptions, the flesh and soul of the Lord are servile and ignorant unless united to the Word of God. Here Cordier wittily puts "intellectual traces" and wrongly reads ἰσχναῖς. Another and common solution is that Christ refers to the Father, as author, what he knows, so that only the Father is said to know what the Son knows only with the Father and as the Father, and knows from him. Gregory so glosses it: the Son does not know the day or hour otherwise than as the Father does. Basil: but the Son did not know, except the Father, for the knowledge was given him by the Father. Cordier's rendering is not apt, and adds no light to Mark's text; nor is his version better on the point Basil urges, which shows the solution is not forced, since "alone" is not added as in Matthew. Cordier: "since the word alone is added, which lies in Matthew"; he means "is placed", and the negation has dropped out, as happens, by a hasty pen or the press. A third solution: these things were said by dispensation, with which the Lord called his disciples away from questions that held more curiosity than necessary use, though he would otherwise explain diligently whatever they asked of such things as had the appearance of love of learning, says Cyril: things having a show of honest desire to know but needing no deeper search. So he passes over the end as convenient, saying he does not know it as man; nor the holy angels in heaven, he says, lest they grieve, being not trusted with what was beyond measure. That is, to trust with the secret, to commit, in Chrysostom on 1 Cor. and others. Henry Stephanus more scrupulously prefers "I dare to commit". Cordier's "lest they be saddened, as if beyond measure dissenting" is unlearned; is it a trouble to review the Greek beside the Latin versions and keep it at hand? Isidore, book 1, epistle 127. It shows no benefit in knowing the day or hour, but the greatest in not knowing: that, thinking every day to be that day, we may be ready for it.

anchorLine: πάντων τῶν κοσμικῶν νοημάτων. Τὸ δὲ κολόβιον (q),
text: (q) Τὸ δὲ κολόβιον. Paucis hic explicat Maximus quod alii plenius prosecuti sunt, de monachorum habitu; in quibus Cass. l. ix, Doroth. et alii colobiorum, quod manus non contegant, iisque abscissæ manicæ sint, hanc et alii significationem afferunt, quo amputatos mundi actus et opera monachis suggerant: linei velaminis indumentum indicio aiunt, ab omni eos terrena conversatione mortificatos. Maximus, moralis philosophiæ cultores, eaque velut contectos; adversus præcipue gulam et venerea, adversus quæ durum monacho certamen. Intextum colobio signum aliquod purpureum, velut belli tesseram, quo summo imperatori militent monachi, auctor est Doroth. doctrina: Ἀναλάβου, paulo aliam formam, quam nostri scapularis (ut vocant) fuisse existimo, quod quasi resticulæ duplices essent atque hinc inde succingerent, etc., apud Cass. c. 16, quæ nostro scapulari non admodum videntur congruere: nisi partes ipsæ astrictæ erant ac ligaculo cohærebant, ut etiamnunc servant Carthusienses: κουκούλλιον etiam Sozom. l. iii, c. 14, σκέπασμα τῆς κεφαλῆς. Maximi ratio ipsa pervia; quod mentem protegat, signum esse divinæ gratiæ prote-
en: Maximus explains briefly here what others treat more fully, on the monks' habit; among them Cassian book 9, Dorotheus and others. Of the colobium, because it does not cover the hands and its sleeves are cut off, others too give this meaning: that it suggests to monks that the acts and works of the world are cut off; they say the linen garment is a sign that they are mortified to all earthly dealings. Maximus, of those who cultivate moral philosophy, and as if covered by it, against gluttony and lust especially, against which the monk has a hard fight. That a purple sign is woven into the colobium, like a battle token by which monks serve the supreme emperor, is attested by Dorotheus in his teaching: Take up. I think it was a somewhat different form from our scapular, since there were as it were double straps girding on each side, etc., in Cassian ch. 16, which do not quite fit our scapular, unless the parts were drawn tight and held together by a tie, as the Carthusians still keep it; also Sozomen, book 3, ch. 14, cowl, a covering of the head. Maximus's reasoning is plain: that it protects the mind, a sign of divine grace protect- [continues].

Οὐ περὶ αὐτῆς τῆς Πεντηκοστῆς (r), ἐν ᾗ τὸ
text: (r) Οὐ περὶ αὐτῆς τῆς Πεντηκοστῆς. Durum plane, sic vocem Πεντηκοστῆς accepisse Lucam: nec admodum cogit illa ratio, quod Paulus genua posuit in oratione: quod non licebat per canones a Paschate ad Pentecostem, ob memoriam resurrectionis Dominicæ. Sive enim jam exstabant illi canones, sive sequentium pastorum sedulitate augendo divino cultui, Ecclesia jam constituta atque adulta, conditi sunt; nihil tamen illi officiebant, quin Paulus supremum vale dicturus ac quibus dicebat, presbyteri ac Ecclesiæ primores, sic procumberent, eoque corporis gestu et habitu, tum tristitiam vicissim illi suam proderent, tum divinam opem propensiore humilitate deposcerent. Ritus ille non flectendi in publicis statisque Ecclesiæ precibus et officiis locum habet, omnique Græcis religione servatur; in aliis nescio an et ipsis inviolabilis sit; quod videtur Maximus innuere. Utut sit, passim legimus in Scriptura sic procubuisse orantes, cum majoris aliquid compunctionis, exorando divinam clementiam, ostendere vellent. Sic bene Chrysost. inde oras[s]e colligit, οὐχ ἁπλῶς, ἀλλὰ μετὰ πολλῆς τῆς κατανύξεως· Non defunctorie ac quavis ratione, sed cum magna compunctione, θεὶς τὰ γόνατα αὐτοῦ σὺν πᾶσιν αὐτοῖς· ponens ipse genua cum illis omnibus. Quin sacer ipse textus, egisse Paulum festum Azymorum Philippis, in procinctu hujus itineris, clare loquitur: Ἡμεῖς δὲ ἐξεπλεύσαμεν μετὰ τὰς ἡμέρας τῶν Ἀζύμων ἀπὸ Φιλίππου. Ex quo Chrys. Καὶ γὰρ τὰς ἑορτὰς ἐμοὶ δοκεῖ σπουδάζειν αὐτὸν ποιεῖν ἐν ταῖς μεγάλαις πόλεσι· Hoc puto studebat, ut solemnitates in magnis urbibus perageret. Atque adeo, uti Philippis Pascha dieque Azymorum egerat, sic Pentecosten Hierosolymis celebrare satagebat. Œcumenius ipse non satis accuratus, illa verba Act. xxi, 5: Ὅτε δὲ ἐγένετο ἡμᾶς ἐξαρτίσαι τὰς ἡμέρας, completis diebus, de diebus Azymorum exponit, τουτέστι, μετὰ τὰ Ἄζυμα, cum sermo sit de septem diebus, quos Tyri egit Paulus cum discipulis, peractis jam diebus Azymorum Philippis, Act. xx, 6. Ac neque si de diebus Azymorum ibi sermo esset, quidquam locus auctori faveret, cum statim sequatur alia precantis Pauli et fidelium geniculatio, Καὶ θέντες τὰ γόνατα, ἐπὶ τὸν αἰγιαλὸν προσηυξάμεθα. Positis genibus, in littore oravimus; cum τῆς πεντηκοστῆς (paschalis scilicet temporis) non nisi septem circiter dies effluxissent, nec tempus τῶν νηστειῶν esset.
en: It is hard to say that Luke took the word Pentecost in this sense, and the reason that Paul knelt in prayer, because the canons forbade it from Easter to Pentecost in memory of the Lord's resurrection, is not very compelling. Whether those canons already existed or were made later by the care of the pastors to increase worship when the Church was established and grown, they did not prevent Paul, about to say his last farewell, and the elders and leaders of the Church from kneeling, and by that posture showing their sorrow and begging divine help with more earnest humility. The rite of not kneeling holds in public and fixed prayers and offices of the Church and is kept by the Greeks as a religious duty; I do not know whether it is inviolable among others, which Maximus seems to hint. However that may be, we read throughout Scripture of people praying prostrate when they wished to show some deeper compunction in begging divine mercy. So Chrysostom rightly infers that he prayed not casually but with great compunction, kneeling with them all. Indeed the sacred text itself plainly says that Paul kept the feast of Unleavened Bread at Philippi, on the eve of this journey: "we sailed away after the days of Unleavened Bread from Philippi." From which Chrysostom: "for it seems to me he took pains to keep the feasts in great cities"; I think he aimed to celebrate the solemnities in great cities. So as he had kept Passover and the days of Unleavened Bread at Philippi, he was eager to keep Pentecost at Jerusalem. Oecumenius himself is not accurate enough, taking the words of Acts 21:5 ("when the days were completed") as about the days of Unleavened Bread, that is, after the Unleavened Bread, when the talk is of the seven days Paul spent at Tyre with the disciples, the days of Unleavened Bread having already been spent at Philippi (Acts 20:6). And even if the days of Unleavened Bread were meant there, the passage would not help the author, since there follows another kneeling of Paul at prayer and of the faithful: "kneeling on the beach we prayed." Having knelt on the shore we prayed, though scarcely seven days of Pentecost (the Paschal season) had passed, and it was not the time of fasts.

ζούσης τὸν ἄνθρωπον (s)· ζημιούσης δὲ τοῦ προλα-
text: (s) Καὶ σῳζούσης τὸν ἄνθρωπον. Nihil Maximus in hac ardua quæstione ac Apostoli loco, quam quod superiores Græci theologi. Eorum princeps Chrys. hom. 9 in I Cor. i, ubi serio gehennam esse perpetuam, nec pœnas damnatorum unquam interituras, asseruit; ne quis ex his Pauli verbis, assumptaque illi similitudine pœnis tandem se liberandum, ac salutem adepturum putaret; de fidelibus sermonem esse ostendit, qui vitam (virtutes scilicet aut vitia) superædificent, proque ejus ratione recipiant. Qui cum recta fide virtute fulserunt, manente quod superædificaverunt, laudem referant, illorum manifestata virtute. At qui vitio sorduerunt, ζημιωθήσεται· ἰδοὺ μία κόλασις· αὐτὸς δὲ σωθήσεται, οὕτως ὡς διὰ πυρός· ἰδοὺ καὶ δευτέρα· Detrimentum patietur: ecce unum supplicium: ipse autem salvus erit, sic quasi per ignem: ecce et alterum. Magisque sequentibus explicat: Ὃ δὲ λέγει, τοῦτό ἐστιν· Οὐχὶ καὶ αὐτὸς οὕτω ἀπολεῖται, ὡς τὰ ἔργα, εἰς τὸ μηδὲν χωρῶν· ἀλλὰ μενεῖ ἐν τῷ πυρί· Quod vero ait, istud est: Non etiam ipse sic peribit, quemadmodum opera, ut in nihilum cedat; sed manebit in igne. Probatque ex usu communis sermonis, quo servari in igne dicimus, quæ in eo non comburuntur, nec statim in cinerem rediguntur. Quidquid denique istud est, dictum esse ad terrorem divini judicii peccantibus incutiendum. Itaque τὸ, σωθήσεται, quasi καταχρηστικῶς, pro τηρηθήσεται, quod et reddit Theoph. ipse eamdem Chrys. expositionem perstringens: Ἀλλὰ σωθήσεται, τουτέστι σῶος τηρηθήσεται, ὥστε καὶ τῷ πυρὶ κατακαίεσθαι. Σώζεται μέντοι αὐτός, ὁ ἁμαρτωλὸς δηλαδή, τουτέστι σῶος τηρεῖται δίκας αἰωνίους ὑπέχων· Sed servabitur; pro eo ac dicat, remanebit incolumis, ut et igni comburatur. Servabitur tamen ipse (peccator scilicet), hoc est manebit integer pœnas æternas sustinens. Auctor Exposit. in Scripturam, t. II, Athan. qu. 100: Ζημιωθήσεται τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν· σωθήσεται δὲ αὐτός, ὡς διὰ πυρός· τουτέστι σῶος καὶ ἀκέραιος μενεῖ ἐν τῷ πυρί, καὶ οὐχ ὄψεται θάνατον, ἀλλὰ τὸ ἔργον αὐτοῦ μόνον κατακαήσεται καὶ χαωθήσεται· αὐτὸς δὲ ἀκέραιος μενεῖ εἰς αἰῶνας κολαζόμενος, καὶ οὐ διαλυθήσεται· Damnum patietur regni cœlorum. Salvus vero fiet ipse, tanquam per ignem; hoc est, salvus manebit et integer in igne, nec videbit mortem; sed opus ipsius solummodo comburetur: ipse vero integer manebit in sæculum sæculi ignis pœnam luens, nec unquam dissolvetur. Theodoret. ac doctorem refert: ac sane ad eum videtur collineare tota mens Apostoli; cujus opus maneat, vel ardeat, non quod ipse, sed quod discipuli superædificantes, ipsi se fecerint, accepta ab eo doctrina, beneque aut male utentes, quorum interitus, nullam ei labem inferat, quod ipse non ejus auctor sit, sed ipsimet: Εἴ τινος τὸ ἔργον κατακαήσεται, ζημιωθήσεται, οὕτω δὲ ὡς διὰ πυρός· αὐτὸς δὲ σωθήσεται, τουτέστιν ὁ διδάσκαλος· οὐ γὰρ αἴτιος τῆς τούτων ἐπὶ τὸ χεῖρον τροπῆς· Si cujus opus arserit, damnum accipiet, sic vero quasi per ignem: ipse vero salvabitur, nempe doctor. Quod eorum mutationis in deterius auctor minime exstiterit. Sin autem, inquit, aliquis nolit illud, quasi per ignem, operi aptare, sed doctori, sic intelligat: Ὅτι ὑπὲρ μὲν ἐκείνων οὐκ εἰσπραχθήσεται δίκας· σωθήσεται δὲ καὶ αὐτὸς διὰ πυρὸς δοκιμαζόμενος, εἴπερ ἄρα ἔχει τὸν βίον τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ κατάλληλον· Non dabit pro eis pœnas; verum ipse etiam salvabitur, per ignem probatus, num vitam convenientem doctrinæ habeat. A quo non longe abest Isid. l. v, epist. 84: Ὁ πάντα τὰ εἰς αὐτὸν ἥκοντα πληρώσας, εἰς τὸ πεῖσαι, καὶ μὴ πείσας, ὡς ἀνύσας, δίκαιο[ς] ἂν εἴη θαυμάζεσθαι. Τοσοῦτον ἀπέχει τοῦ μέμφεσθαι ἄξιος εἶναι· Qui pro munere ac officii ratione omnia implet, ut persuadeat, nec tamen persuadet, ac si rem peregisset, merito laudem habet ac admirationem; tantum abest ut ulli reprehensioni obnoxius sit. Ubi nescio quis imperite vel interpres vel typogr. Tantum abest ut reprehensione videatur dignus, ut omnis sit expers.
en: Maximus says nothing in this hard question and Pauline passage beyond what the earlier Greek theologians said. Their chief, Chrysostom (hom. 9 on 1 Cor. 1), insists that Gehenna is eternal and the punishments of the damned will never end, lest anyone think from Paul's words and the image he uses that he will at last be freed and saved. He shows the talk is of believers who build on the foundation a life of virtues or vices and receive according to it. Those who shone in right faith and virtue keep what they built and win praise; those stained by vice suffer loss: that is one punishment; and he is saved as through fire: that is a second. He explains further that the man will not perish as the works do, passing into nothing, but will remain in the fire. He proves this from common speech, in which we say things are kept in the fire when they are not burned up or reduced at once to ash. Whatever it means, it is said to frighten sinners with divine judgment. So "will be saved" is used loosely for "will be kept", as Theophylact renders it, summarizing the same exposition of Chrysostom: he is kept safe, so as even to be burned in the fire, and he is kept safe bearing eternal punishments. The author of the Exposition on Scripture (Athanasius, vol. 2, q. 100) says: he will lose the kingdom of heaven but be saved as through fire, that is, he will remain safe and whole in the fire, and will not see death; only his work will be burned up; he will remain whole for ever, punished, and not dissolved. Theodoret refers it to the teacher: the whole mind of the Apostle seems to aim at him; whether the work of the disciples who build on his teaching, using it well or badly, stands or burns, their ruin brings no stain on him, since he is not its author but they themselves. If anyone's work is burned he will suffer loss, yet as through fire; but he, the teacher, will be saved, for he is not the cause of their turn for the worse. If anyone will not apply "as through fire" to the work but to the teacher, let him understand: he will not be called to account for them, but will himself be saved, tried by fire, if his life fits his teaching. Near this is Isidore, book 5, epistle 84: he who has done all that belongs to him to persuade, and has not persuaded, is as one who has succeeded and is rightly admired; he is so far from blame as to be worthy. Here some unskilled interpreter or printer [has gone astray]: "So far is he from deserving reproach that he is wholly free of it."

anchorLine: Τοῦτο εἴρηται ἀντὶ τοῦ, Θρηνήσουσι καὶ κόψον-|ται (t), εἰς μετάνοιαν ἐρχόμενοι
text: (t) Ἀντὶ τοῦ, Θρηνήσουσι καὶ κόψονται. Hujus sic novæ acceptionis vocis illius, ἀποκόψωνται, meminit et Hesych. exque illo Var. ἀποκοπησαμένη, σ[τ]ερνοκοπησαμένη, ἀποκοψαμένη. Plangens tundensque pectus. Hæc forte sic mitis excogitata expositio, ne quid austerius habere imprecatio hæc, quam pro Apostoli mansuetudine, videretur: reliqui tamen sic exponunt, ut quasi immedicabiliter ægrotantibus summeque aliis exitiosis, et ἀστατοῦσι (eos qui liberi essent et ad supernam spectarent Jerusalem, quasi vagos exsulesque ac captivos circumducentibus) non περιτομήν (circumcisionem qua gloriabantur) sed plenam ἀποτομήν et ἀποκοπήν (virilium scilicet excisionem) justa eis æmulatione imprecetur; quod est, nullam deinceps sic malæ gentis fore sobolem. Videtur Hesych. quod ita refert, in aliquo comico, ac de muliere dictum, legisse: qui sexus ad planctum pectusque tundendum maxime proclivis est.
en: "Instead of: they will mourn and strike themselves." Hesychius also mentions this new sense of the word apokopsontai, and from him come the variants apokopesamene, sternokopesamene, apokopsamene: "beating and striking the breast." This mild exposition was perhaps devised so that the imprecation would not seem harsher than the Apostle's gentleness allows. Others, however, explain it thus: to those who are incurably sick and ruinous to others, and who unsettle (those who were free and looked to the Jerusalem above, as if wandering, exiled and captive), he wishes not circumcision, in which they gloried, but a full cutting off, the excision of the virile parts, by a just retaliation; that is, that no offspring of such a bad race should come after. Hesychius seems to report that he read this in some comic poet, said of a woman, whose sex is most inclined to lamenting and beating the breast.

anchorLine: τρός (u)· Ἀμμανίτης δὲ, πατὴρ μητρός· σημαί-
text: (u) Ἔντερον πατρός. Non satis videtur istud etymum accuratum; nota enim nominis Moab derivatio seu origo; quod ex patre (Lot scilicet) post Sodomorum subversionem, per filiarum fraudem incestuoso concubitu natus sit. Num ergo scripserit Maximus, ὧν ἐκ τοῦ πατρός, quod ita imperitus scriba in ἔντερον verterit? Sed quod eam ipsam vocem iterum repetit, inque ea vim facit, sic nos opinari non sinit. Nec minus clara etymologia nominis Ammon, ex quo Ammanitæ seu Ammonitæ, ex secunda Loti filia ipsoque Loto, perscripta Gen. xix, 38: Filius populi mei; nec occurrit, unde Maximo, τὸ πατὴρ μητρός obrepserit. Quod etiam de tertia et quarta generatione huc translatum est, ad alia spectat Exod. xx, 5; Num. xiv, 18; Deut. v, 9 de his qui transgrediuntur divina mandata, quibus Deus comminatur se redditurum in tertiam et quartam generationem, et in sæculum (id est, nunquam) admittendos in Ecclesiam Domini, Moabitas et Ammonitas, divina sententia est. Fefellit parum attentum memoria, quod de Idumæis et Ægyptiis, Deut. xxiii, 7, in contrarium sancitur; post tertiam generationem intraturos in Ecclesiam Domini, nec esse abominandos eos populos, quod Idumæus ejus frater esset, ex ea idem Abrahæ stirpe (ipsa Esau progenies) oriundus; ac quod Ægyptius Hebræos hospites ac colonos habuisset atque fovisset. Admitti in Ecclesiam Domini, putem, consiliorum gentis esse participem, illiusque plene jura nancisci, ac quasi verum Judæum haberi, non ad eorum transeuntem cultum, inter proselytas ac fideles admitti. Verum hæc alterius loci sint et communicationis. Vocem Ammanitas deduxerit Maximus ab אמן, quod est nutrivit, ex vocis sonique affinitate dece-
en: "Intestine of the father." This etymology does not seem exact enough; for the derivation of the name Moab is known: he was born of his father (Lot) after the destruction of Sodom, by the daughters' trick, in incestuous union. Did Maximus then write "of those from the father", and an unskilled scribe turn it into "intestine"? But that he repeats the same word and presses on it forbids us to think so. The etymology of the name Ammon, from which Ammanites or Ammonites, from Lot's second daughter and Lot himself, set down in Gen. 19:38 as "son of my people", is no less clear; nor is it clear how "father of a mother" crept in to Maximus. As for the third and fourth generation carried over here, it looks to other passages (Exod. 20:5; Num. 14:18; Deut. 5:9) about those who transgress the divine commands, against whom God threatens to repay to the third and fourth generation; that Moabites and Ammonites are to be admitted into the Church of the Lord not even for ever (that is, never) is a divine decree. Memory failed the careless reader, since Deut. 23:7 lays down the opposite for Edomites and Egyptians: after the third generation they enter the assembly of the Lord, and are not to be abhorred, because the Edomite is his brother, sprung from the same stock of Abraham (Esau's own line), and because the Egyptian had sheltered and cherished the Hebrews as guests and settlers. To be admitted into the Church of the Lord, I would think, is to share the counsels of the nation and to gain its full rights, and to be counted as a true Jew, not admitted among proselytes and believers passing over to their worship. But these belong to another place and discussion. Maximus may have derived the word Ammanites from the Hebrew word for "nourished", from likeness of sound [...]

text: ptus; quod et Hieronymo quandoque obrepsisse notavit Morinus in Exercit. Bibl. Porro in his Maximi quæstionibus non desunt aliqua, quæ majorem ἀκρίβειαν, etiam in eo genere quod libens assectatur, τῆς ἀλληγορίας sensusque spiritalis, videantur exigere: ut quædam mihi su-spicio sit, vel quasi inchoatum quoddam ejus opus esse, quidquid istud est, vel aliena manu auctum et interpolatum, ut fere contingit in scriptis hujus generis, ubi nihil cohæret; sed sunt quæsita prout memoriæ occurrebant, nullo certo ordine aut methodo, hinc inde congesta.
en: [...] which Morin also noted had sometimes crept in for Jerome, in his Biblical Exercitations. Furthermore, in these Questions of Maximus there are some points that seem to demand greater exactness, even in the kind he gladly pursues, allegory and the spiritual sense. So I have a suspicion that this is either an unfinished work of his, whatever it is, or one enlarged and interpolated by another hand, as usually happens in writings of this kind where nothing coheres; but the questions are gathered as they came to memory, in no fixed order or method, heaped together from here and there.
